JSON: Name: genz_heritage_erp_pipeline Title: Mixed-method assessment using questionnaires and event-related potentials to determine Generation Z preferences for cultural heritage landscapes Short Hypothesis: Viewing images of religious and traditional folk heritage landscapes causes higher explicit preference ratings and produces larger P200 and LPP amplitudes but smaller N200 amplitudes in Generation Z participants than viewing industrial and historical urban heritage landscape images. Related Work: Existing approaches to measuring tourism and heritage preferences rely predominantly on self-report instruments (surveys, Likert scales, interviews) that quantify explicit attitudes, intentions, and place attachment but are subject to recall bias, social desirability, and limited temporal resolution. Separate strands of cognitive neuroscience research use EEG/ERP to index rapid attention and affective responses (components such as P100, P200, N200, LPP) in visual and consumer contexts; these methods provide high temporal resolution but have been used sparingly in heritage and tourism research and often with small samples, limited stimulus control, or without integrated behavioral measures. Prior multimodal or mixed-method attempts are limited by lack of theoretical integration (few apply dual-process frameworks), inconsistent component selection and time windows, inadequate control for low-level visual confounds, and scarce evaluation of mediators (place imagination, awe) and moderators (visual esthetics). Cross-generational and cross-cultural generalizability is underexplored. Abstract: This project defines a structured pipeline that combines questionnaire-based explicit measures with EEG-derived event-related potentials to test how Generation Z forms preferences for cultural heritage landscapes. The approach operationalizes four landscape categories (historical urban, industrial heritage, religious sacred, traditional folk), collects large-sample survey data to quantify place imagination, awe, visual esthetics, and explicit preference, and acquires ERP data using a controlled oddball visual paradigm to measure P100, P200, N200, and LPP responses. The pipeline integrates mediation and moderated-mediation analysis (place imagination → awe → preference; visual esthetics as moderator) with ERP statistical contrasts and classification analyses to link implicit neural markers to explicit choice. Main contributions are: (1) a reproducible experimental protocol for mixed explicit–implicit preference assessment; (2) specification of analysis windows and statistical tests for ERP components relevant to heritage evaluation; and (3) an evaluation plan that directly compares survey-only, ERP-only, and combined models. The expected outcome is a validated methodological framework that maps rapid neural processing signatures to behavioral preference variables for Generation Z in heritage contexts. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Survey dataset: online sample of Generation Z participants N>=320 evaluating 40 standardized heritage images (10 per category) on 7-point scales for place imagination, awe, visual esthetics, and preference; control sample non-Generation Z N>=320 for between-group comparison. (B) ERP dataset: laboratory sample of Generation Z participants N>=24 (target 30, expecting >=22 usable) performing an oddball visual task with 40 heritage images (non-target, 85% frequency distributed across four categories) and 10 neutral target images (15%), repeated 5 blocks for ~250 trials. Stimuli balanced for size, luminance, and color histogram. Baselines: (1) questionnaire-only model (mediation analyses), (2) ERP-only model (component amplitude contrasts), (3) combined model (behavioral + ERP predictors), (4) chance/random baseline for classification. Ablation studies: A1 remove visual esthetics moderator from mediation model; A2 remove place imagination mediator; A3 ERP classification using only early components (P100,P200) vs. full set (P100,P200,N200,LPP). Evaluation metrics: explicit: mean preference scores, effect sizes (Cohen’s d), mediation indirect effects with 95% bootstrap CI; ERP: mean amplitudes and latencies per component/time window, repeated-measures ANOVA (heritage_type × electrode), partial eta-squared; correlation (Pearson) between ERP amplitudes and preference; classification: accuracy, AUC, precision/recall via stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Preprocessing and analysis pipeline: EEG acquisition 64-channel Ag/AgCl, sampling 500 Hz; bandpass 0.1–30 Hz; epoch −200 to +1000 ms; baseline correction; ICA for artifact removal; trial rejection threshold; average trials per condition; component windows: P100 80–120 ms (parieto-occipital P1,P2,Pz), P200 150–200 ms (fronto-central F1,F2,Fz,C1,C2,Cz), N200 250–350 ms (fronto-central same sites), LPP 500–600 ms (centro-parietal C1,C2,Cz,P1,P2,Pz). Statistical tests: check normality and sphericity; Greenhouse–Geisser correction where applicable; mediation via PROCESS Model 6 with 5000 bootstrap samples and moderated-mediation via Model 14. Significance threshold alpha=0.05 with FDR correction for multiple comparisons on ERP electrodes/time windows. Report effect sizes and 95% CIs. Data split for classification uses per-subject averaged-trial feature vectors and time-windowed amplitude features. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical EEG failure modes: excessive artifacts or high trial rejection rates reducing usable ERP data and statistical power; ICA misclassification removing neural signal. Sample and generalization biases: Generation Z sample may be non-representative (regional, cultural), limiting external validity; results may not generalize beyond the Jingdezhen-based stimuli set. Stimulus confounds: residual low-level visual differences (luminance, contrast, spatial frequency) may drive ERP differences despite preprocessing. Causal inference limits: cross-sectional survey plus passive ERP cannot establish long-term preference causality or behavior in real-world visitation. Statistical risks: multiple comparisons across electrodes and time windows increase false positives if corrections are insufficient; mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding. Scalability and compute: high-throughput EEG preprocessing and bootstrap mediation require substantial compute for larger samples. Ecological validity: laboratory visual presentation and oddball task may not reflect multisensory, interactive, in-situ heritage experiences. Small ERP sample sizes constrain ability to detect small-to-moderate effects and to train stable predictive classifiers.
